level1.text: A power plant feeds $500\,\text{MWh}$ of electrical energy into the electricity grid in a day. In the grid, $4.0\,\%$ of the sent energy is lost. How much energy arrives? Give your answer in megawatt-hours.

The figure shows the energy flows of the electricity grid and the district heating network. A heating plant feeds $360\,\text{MWh}$ of thermal energy into the district heating network in a week. Read from the figure what share of the energy sent into the district heating network is lost. How much energy is lost in the network during the week? Give your answer in megawatt-hours.
$80.0\,\text{MWh}$ of electricity is sent into the national grid, and $76.8\,\text{MWh}$ reaches the users. What is the efficiency of the transfer? Give your answer as a percentage.
A power plant feeds an electric power of $125\,\text{MW}$ into the network, and $4.0\,\%$ of the sent power is lost in the network. How much power arrives? Give your answer in megawatts.
Heat escapes steadily from a district heating pipe into the surroundings at a power of $2.5\,\text{kW}$. How much energy is lost in a day? Give your answer in kilowatt-hours.
Why is electrical energy transmitted at a high voltage in the national grid?
level1.answer: For the same power, a smaller current is enough, so the conductors heat up less and the loss becomes smaller.

choices.text: High voltage increases the energy produced by the power plant, so the losses do not matter.
choices.feedback: Voltage does not add energy. A transformer changes the voltage but does not produce energy, and the losses are reduced precisely because there would otherwise be a lot of them.

choices.text: At a high voltage, energy is not converted into heat on the way at all, so no loss occurs.
choices.feedback: The loss becomes smaller but does not disappear completely: in the electricity grid, about $4\,\%$ of the sent energy is still lost, because the current always heats the conductors to some extent.

choices.text: For the same power, a smaller current is enough, so the conductors heat up less and the loss becomes smaller.
choices.feedback: Correct: when the voltage is high, the same power is transmitted with a smaller current. A smaller current heats the conductors less, so less electrical energy is converted into heat in the transmission.

choices.text: High voltage makes electricity travel faster in the wire, so less heat has time to form.
choices.feedback: The cause of the loss is the heating of the conductor as current flows, not the travel time. High voltage helps because the current is smaller.

level1.text: $250\,\text{MWh}$ of electrical energy is sent into a regional electricity grid in a day, and $238\,\text{MWh}$ reaches the users. What share of the sent energy is lost? Give your answer as a percentage.

A power of $800\,\text{kW}$ is sent from a heating plant into a district heating pipe, and a power of $728\,\text{kW}$ reaches the property. How much power is lost in the pipe? Give your answer in kilowatts.

level2.text: In a poorly insulated district heating network, $20\,\%$ of the energy sent into the network is lost, and $600\,\text{MWh}$ reaches the customers in a week. How much energy is lost in the network in a week? Give your answer in megawatt-hours.

A district of the city needs $1.20\,\text{GWh}$ of heat per week. The efficiency of the old district heating network is $80\,\%$. How much energy must the heating plant feed into the network per week? Give your answer in megawatt-hours.

$2.40\,\text{TWh}$ of electrical energy is fed into the electricity grid of a region in a year (an example situation), and $4.0\,\%$ of the sent energy is lost in the grid. What is the average power of the losses, when a year has $8760\,\text{h}$? Give your answer in megawatts.

A building needs district heating steadily at a power of $40.0\,\text{kW}$. In the old district heating network $20\,\%$ of the sent power is lost. How much energy must the heating plant feed into the network in a day for this building? Give your answer in kilowatt-hours.

The table contains an example data set from the district heating network of a city district: the thermal energy fed into the network by the heating plant and the thermal energy that reached customers in four months.

a) Calculate the share of the energy fed into the network that is lost over the whole period. Give your answer as a percentage.

b) Calculate the share lost in each month and state in which month it is greatest. Give a possible explanation.

a) Deduce from the table how the loss power changes when the voltage is doubled, and estimate the loss power at a voltage of $320\,\text{kV}$. Give your answer in megawatts.

b) Explain briefly in writing why a high voltage reduces the loss.

level2.text: A student writes: “Electricity travels along the wire at the speed of light, so no losses occur in the transmission of electricity.” Which of the following corrects the claim?
level2.answer: Electricity travels quickly, but the current heats the conductor and part of the energy is converted into heat.

choices.text: The claim is correct, because energy that travels quickly does not have time to change into anything else on the way.
choices.feedback: The cause of the loss is not the duration of the transfer. When current flows in a conductor, the conductor heats up and part of the electrical energy is converted into heat, even though the transfer is fast.

choices.text: Electricity travels slowly in the wire, so a large part of the electrical energy has time to break down on the way.
choices.feedback: The loss does not depend on how fast the electrical energy is transferred. It depends on how much the conductor heats up as current flows.

choices.text: Part of the energy disappears completely on the way, even though electricity travels quickly in the wire.
choices.feedback: Energy does not disappear. The lost energy is converted into heat in the surroundings, but the user cannot make use of it.

choices.text: Electricity travels quickly, but the current heats the conductor and part of the energy is converted into heat.
choices.feedback: Correct: the loss occurs when the current heats the conductors, and this heat does not reach the user. That is why less energy arrives than is sent.

level3.text: The customers of a district heating network need $600\,\text{MWh}$ of heat per week. The loss of the network is $9.0\,\%$ of the sent energy. The insulation of the pipes is improved, and the loss decreases to $6.0\,\%$. How much less energy must the heating plant feed into the network per week? Give your answer in megawatt-hours.

Two district heating networks serve similar customers. $500\,\text{MWh}$ is sent into network A per week, and its efficiency is $91.0\,\%$. $520\,\text{MWh}$ is sent into network B per week, and its efficiency is $85.0\,\%$. Which network brings more heat to customers and how many megawatt-hours more? Give the size of the difference in megawatt-hours as your answer.

The loss power of a district heating pipework is steadily $150\,\text{kW}$. The heating of one detached house uses $20\,\text{MWh}$ in a year. The annual loss of the pipework equals the annual heating energy of how many houses, when a year has $8760\,\text{h}$?

The table contains an example data set of the average power of the heat losses of a detached house during the heating season, by building part. The house gets its heat from a district heating network whose loss is $9.0\,\%$ of the sent energy. The heating season is $5000\,\text{h}$. Three improvements are considered: A) insulating the external walls reduces the loss power of the walls by $50\,\%$, B) replacing the windows reduces the loss power of the windows by $40\,\%$, and C) extra insulation of the upper floor reduces the loss power of the upper floor by $60\,\%$.

a) Calculate the thermal energy that each improvement saves in the house during the heating season and choose the improvement that saves the most.

b) How much less energy must the heating plant feed into the network during the heating season when the house carries out this improvement? Give your answer in megawatt-hours.

c) Justify your choice in writing, and explain why the saving of the heating plant is greater than the saving of the house.

data.caption: Average power of the heat losses of the house during the heating season (example data set)

level3.text:
The table contains an example data set of one day of a regional electricity grid: the average power fed into the grid and the share of the energy fed in during the period that is lost.

a) Calculate the energy fed into the grid during the day and the energy lost in it. What share of the energy fed in during the whole day is lost? Give your answer as a percentage.

b) Compare the result with the loss of about $4\,\%$ in the Finnish electricity grid (Finnish Energy, 2024).

c) In which period is the lost energy greatest? Explain in writing why the share of the loss increases when the grid is loaded more. Hint: when the current doubles, the loss power becomes about four times as great.
